title: Optimize vector search in Azure Database for PostgreSQL

questions.q: Azure Database for PostgreSQL runs on SSD storage, but the planner keeps choosing sequential scans for vector queries. Which setting does Learn suggest lowering to 1.1–1.5?

options.text: effective_io_concurrency
options.why: Learn suggests raising effective_io_concurrency to 200, not lowering it.

options.text: random_page_cost
options.why: Correct. The default 4.0 assumes spinning disks; lower values encourage index scans on SSD.

options.text: work_mem
options.why: work_mem affects sorts and hashes, not this cost estimate.

options.text: shared_buffers
options.why: shared_buffers is the cache size, not a cost estimate.

questions.hint: The planner thinks random reads are expensive, a default meant for spinning disks.
questions.explain: random_page_cost tells the planner how expensive random reads are compared with sequential reads.

questions.q: What is the default value of hnsw.ef_search?

options.why: Correct. The default ef_search is 40.
16 is the default HNSW m (connections per node).
200 is at the high-accuracy end of the suggested range.
1 is the default for ivfflat.probes.

questions.hint: The default HNSW search list size is a small round number.
questions.explain: Increase ef_search to 100–200 for high accuracy; lower it to about 20 for latency-critical apps.

questions.q: A server handles 300 concurrent connections. A developer wants to set work_mem to 256 MB globally so vector sorts stop spilling. What's the risk?

options.text: work_mem is just a planner hint and has no effect on sorts
options.why: That describes effective_cache_size.

options.text: Azure ignores work_mem changes above 64 MB
options.why: Learn doesn't describe such a cap.

options.text: It applies per operation per connection, so total use can explode
options.why: Correct. Raise it per session or transaction for vector queries instead.

options.text: Higher work_mem lowers the cache hit ratio below 99% immediately
options.why: Learn ties the hit ratio to shared_buffers, not work_mem.

questions.hint: work_mem is allocated per sort or hash, in every connection.
questions.explain: Use SET work_mem (or SET LOCAL) for the sessions that need it.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A team tunes memory for a dedicated vector search server.

rows.text: A buffer cache hit ratio below 99% can mean shared_buffers is too small.
rows.why: Learn uses <99% as a sign shared_buffers may be too small.

rows.text: effective_cache_size allocates memory for PostgreSQL's cache.
rows.why: It's a planner hint and doesn't allocate memory.

rows.text: The default random_page_cost of 4.0 is tuned for SSD storage.
rows.why: 4.0 reflects spinning disks; use 1.1–1.5 on Azure's SSDs.

rows.text: Inner product (<#>) is the cheapest operator but needs normalized vectors to be meaningful.
rows.why: Inner product is fastest and requires pre-normalized vectors.

questions.hint: A low cache hit ratio means more memory is needed. One parameter only hints at the OS cache.
questions.explain: Measure cache hits and IO, then size shared_buffers; remember which settings are hints.

questions.q: After loading 800,000 new products, EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows Seq Scan on a query that used the vector index yesterday. The operator class matches and LIMIT is present. What should you try first?

options.text: Raise random_page_cost to 4.0
options.why: Raising it discourages index scans.

options.text: Drop the vector index and rebuild it with IVFFlat
options.why: Switching index types doesn't fix stale statistics.

options.text: Run ANALYZE on the table to refresh statistics
options.why: Correct. Outdated statistics after big data changes can make the planner skip the index.

options.text: Set ivfflat.probes to its default of 1
options.why: probes doesn't influence whether the planner uses an index.

questions.hint: The table changed a lot, and the planner is using old row counts.
questions.explain: Stale statistics, large result shares and operator mismatches are the common reasons an index is skipped.

questions.q: Vector queries on a dedicated search server keep reading index pages from disk. The cache hit ratio is 94%. Which parameter should you look at?

options.text: random_page_cost, so that disk reads become cheaper
options.why: That changes the planner's cost estimates, not how much data stays in memory.

options.text: work_mem, so that each sort gets more memory
options.why: work_mem helps sorts and hashes avoid spilling, not cache hits on index pages.

options.text: shared_buffers, PostgreSQL's shared page cache
options.why: Correct. A hit ratio below 99% on vector workloads suggests shared_buffers may be too small.

options.text: max_connections, so that fewer sessions compete
options.why: Connection count doesn't size the shared cache.

questions.hint: Which parameter sizes the memory cache that every session reads data pages from?
questions.explain: shared_buffers controls PostgreSQL's shared memory cache. For vector workloads, it should hold the vector indexes and hot data; a hit ratio below 99% suggests it's too small. Azure tunes it by tier, within an allowed range.

questions.q: After you raise hnsw.ef_search on a shared server, product search improves, but nightly reports on the same server get slower. Which best practice from Learn does this show?

options.text: Disable the vector index during report runs
options.why: That would break product search instead of addressing the trade-off.

options.text: Set every memory parameter to its maximum for the tier
options.why: Maximum values aren't a tuning strategy, and they risk memory problems.

options.text: Monitor for regressions in other workloads
options.why: Correct. Parameters that help vector search can harm other workloads, so watch overall system health after changes.

options.text: Leave parameters at their defaults on a shared server
options.why: Learn encourages tuning, with measurement and monitoring.

questions.hint: A change helped one workload and hurt another.
questions.explain: Best practices: measure with EXPLAIN ANALYZE and Azure Monitor, monitor for regressions because vector tuning can hurt other workloads, and document what you changed and why.

questions.q: A recommendation engine with two million products must reach 99%+ recall at low latency, the data is mostly read, and memory is ample. Which index fits best?

options.text: A B-tree on the embedding
options.why: B-tree indexes don't support vector similarity.

options.text: An HNSW index
options.why: Correct. HNSW gives 99%+ recall and consistent latency for read-mostly workloads.

options.text: No index (sequential scan)
options.why: Over 1M rows an index is essential.

options.text: An IVFFlat index
options.why: IVFFlat has a lower recall ceiling.

questions.hint: High recall, mostly reads, plenty of memory: the graph-based index.
questions.explain: HNSW for high recall and read-mostly data; IVFFlat when memory or build time is tight.

questions.q: For a table with 5,000 rows of embeddings, what does Learn say about a vector index?

options.text: DiskANN is the one index that works at this size
options.why: DiskANN targets very large datasets.

options.text: It's essential; queries are unusable without one
options.why: That's the guidance for more than one million rows.

options.text: HNSW can't be built on fewer than 10,000 rows
options.why: HNSW can even be built on an empty table.

options.text: Its benefit is limited; a sequential scan may be fast enough
options.why: Correct. Under 10,000 rows, the benefit is limited.

questions.hint: With very few rows, scanning them all may already be fast enough.
questions.explain: Index benefit grows with table size: limited under 10k, essential above 1M.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. An HNSW index is created with `m = 16, ef_construction = 64`.

rows.text: ef_construction of 64 meets Learn's guidance of at least 2 × m.
Raising ef_construction later changes query time without rebuilding.
rows.why: Changing m or ef_construction requires rebuilding; ef_construction affects build time and quality.

rows.text: Raising hnsw.ef_search at query time doesn't require a rebuild.

questions.hint: ef_construction should be at least twice m. Build settings need a rebuild; query settings don't.
questions.explain: Build-time parameters (m, ef_construction) need a rebuild; ef_search is set per session.

questions.q: A catalog reloads large batches of products every night, and the database has limited memory. Which index type does Learn suggest?

options.text: No index
options.why: Large catalogs still need an index for interactive queries.

options.text: HNSW with m = 64
options.why: Higher m increases memory, which is limited here.

options.text: IVFFlat
options.why: Correct. IVFFlat suits limited memory and frequent bulk updates, with faster builds.

options.text: HNSW with ef_construction = 400
options.why: Higher ef_construction lengthens builds further.

questions.hint: Frequent rebuilds and little memory favor the index that builds fast and stores centroids.
questions.explain: IVFFlat trades some recall for lower memory and faster builds.

questions.q: You must build a vector index on a busy production table without blocking writes, and track its progress. Which two actions are correct? (Select two.)

options.text: Use REINDEX INDEX without CONCURRENTLY
options.why: Plain REINDEX blocks writes.

options.text: Temporarily set ivfflat.probes to 1
options.why: probes is a query-time setting unrelated to builds.

options.text: Use CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY
options.why: Correct. CONCURRENTLY allows writes during the build.

options.text: Watch pg_stat_progress_create_index
options.why: Correct. It shows phase, blocks and tuples done.

questions.hint: Build without blocking writes, and use a system view to follow the build.
questions.explain: Index builds lock writes by default; CONCURRENTLY takes longer but avoids downtime.

questions.q: You created an HNSW index a month ago, but you suspect queries aren't using it. Which check does Learn describe?

options.text: Run ANALYZE and assume the index is used afterwards
options.why: ANALYZE refreshes statistics, but it doesn't tell you whether the index was used.

options.text: Query pg_stat_user_indexes and look at idx_scan for the index
options.why: Correct. Low idx_scan counts suggest the index isn't being used, so check the operator class.

options.text: Compare the index size with the table size
options.why: Size doesn't show whether queries use the index.

options.text: Check pg_stat_progress_create_index for the index
options.why: That view tracks index builds in progress, not later usage.

questions.hint: PostgreSQL keeps usage counters for each index.
questions.explain: Check index health with pg_stat_user_indexes: pg_relation_size for size, and idx_scan / idx_tup_read for usage. Low idx_scan means the index isn't used; verify the query operator matches the index operator class.

questions.q: Almost every recommendation query includes `WHERE in_stock = true`. Which index reduces size and maintenance for this pattern?

options.text: A partial index with WHERE in_stock = true
options.why: Correct. A partial index covers only in-stock rows and is used for queries with that condition.

options.text: A B-tree index on every column
options.why: Indexing everything raises write and storage costs.

options.text: A second HNSW index on the embedding
options.why: An extra vector index doesn't help this filter.

options.text: A GIN index on the attributes JSONB column
options.why: GIN helps containment queries on JSONB.

questions.hint: Most queries share one condition. An index can cover only those rows.
questions.explain: Partial indexes suit filters that nearly every query shares.

questions.q: Products store price inside a JSONB attributes column with a GIN index, and queries filter `(attributes->>'price')::numeric BETWEEN 100 AND 500`. They're slow. What should you add?

options.text: An expression index on the extracted price
options.why: Correct. An expression index enables range queries on that JSONB field.

options.text: An HNSW index on the attributes JSONB column
options.why: HNSW indexes vectors, not JSONB.

options.text: A second GIN index on the same attributes column
options.why: GIN doesn't accelerate range queries.

options.text: A partial index WHERE price > 0 on the table
options.why: price isn't a column here, and the filter isn't selective.

questions.hint: A GIN index on JSONB doesn't help a numeric range on one extracted value.
questions.explain: GIN serves containment; expression or structured-column B-tree indexes serve ranges.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A products table has a B-tree index on `(category_id, price)` and three vector columns.

rows.text: The index helps WHERE category_id = 5 AND price < 100.
rows.why: Filters on the leftmost columns use the index.

rows.text: The index helps WHERE price < 100 on its own.
One HNSW index can cover all three vector columns.
rows.why: Each vector column needs its own index.

questions.hint: Composite B-trees need their leading column. Each vector column needs its own index.
questions.explain: Composite B-tree indexes serve leading-column filters; vector indexes are per column.

questions.q: User-activity embeddings arrive daily and grow to 80 million rows. Old months are dropped, queries filter by date, and rebuilding one index takes hours. What does Learn suggest?

options.text: Store each day's vectors in a separate database
options.why: Separate databases block cross-day queries and joins.

options.text: Range-partition by date, creating indexes on the parent
options.why: Correct. Date-range partitions prune scans, drop old data easily and keep per-partition indexes manageable.

options.text: Use a single unpartitioned table with a larger HNSW m
options.why: A denser graph makes builds even longer.

options.text: Move all vectors into one JSONB column
options.why: JSONB doesn't hold or index vectors for similarity search.

questions.hint: Huge, growing tables filtered by date, with old data dropped, suit partitioning.
questions.explain: Indexes created on the parent table are created on every partition and can be rebuilt independently.

questions.q: Every recommendation query filters on brand and release year, which are stored inside a JSONB attributes column. The filters are slow. The attributes are known when you design the schema. What does Learn suggest?

options.text: Turn brand and release year into extra vector dimensions
options.why: Vectors capture meaning. Exact filters belong in structured columns.

options.text: Drop the filters and sort by vector distance only
options.why: That changes the results, which isn't acceptable.

options.text: Add more vector indexes on the embedding column
options.why: The bottleneck is the metadata filter, not the vector search.

options.text: Move them into structured columns with B-tree indexes
options.why: Correct. Native columns give efficient B-tree indexes and accurate planner statistics for frequent filters.

questions.hint: Use JSONB for flexible attributes. What should you use for attributes you always filter on?
questions.explain: Structured columns with native types allow efficient B-tree indexes, type safety and accurate statistics. Use them for attributes known at design time that you frequently filter or sort on.

questions.q: Your embedding model can output 768 or 1,536 dimensions, and tests show 768 gives acceptable quality. You also want to catch any inserts from the wrong model. How should you define the column?

options.text: embedding vector, with no dimension, so that any model works
options.why: Without a dimension, mismatched vectors aren't caught at insert time.

options.text: embedding vector(1536), padding the 768 values with zeros
options.why: Padding wastes storage and hides a model mismatch.

options.text: embedding vector(768)
options.why: Correct. Fewer dimensions cut storage and compute, and an explicit size makes mismatched inserts fail.

options.text: embedding JSONB, so that dimensions can vary
options.why: JSONB can't use pgvector operators or vector indexes.

questions.hint: Lower dimensions save cost. A fixed size in the column definition acts as validation.
questions.explain: Lower dimensions reduce storage and computation while keeping reasonable quality for many use cases. Declaring vector(768) validates inserts: vectors with other dimensions fail.

questions.q: How many read replicas can an Azure Database for PostgreSQL primary have?

options.text: Up to ten
options.why: Learn gives a lower number.

options.text: Up to two
options.why: Learn gives a higher number.

options.text: Unlimited
options.why: There's a limit of five.

options.text: Up to five
options.why: Correct. You can create up to five read replicas per primary.

questions.hint: There's a fixed limit on read replicas per primary.
questions.explain: Replicas can be in other regions and each has its own endpoint.

questions.q: A user saves new preferences and the next page shows recommendations based on them. Similarity searches are routed to read replicas. Where should the preference read go?

options.text: To the primary server
options.why: Correct. Replicas apply changes asynchronously; reads needing immediate consistency go to the primary.

options.text: To the closest read replica
options.why: The replica may not have the update yet.

options.text: To any replica, because replication is synchronous
options.why: Replication is asynchronous.

options.text: To the Redis cache with a 60-minute TTL
options.why: A 60-minute cache could serve stale preferences.

questions.hint: Replicas lag slightly. A read that must see the user's own write goes to the primary.
questions.explain: Route staleness-tolerant similarity searches to replicas and read-your-writes queries to the primary.

questions.q: Which two are good caching candidates for a vector recommendation service, according to Learn? (Select two.)

options.text: Embedding lookups for popular products
options.why: Correct. Frequently requested and slow to change.

options.text: Precomputed "similar items" for top products
options.why: Correct. Bounded key space, frequent requests, low change rate.

options.text: Inventory counts that change every second
options.why: Rapidly changing data causes constant invalidation.

options.text: Arbitrary similarity queries with user-typed text
options.why: Arbitrary queries have an infinite key space.

questions.hint: Cache things that are popular and expensive to compute.
questions.explain: Cache what's requested often, changes slowly and has bounded keys.

rows.why: If average CPU is below 30%, consider scaling down.

rows.text: General Purpose might suffice if memory use stays low.
rows.why: Consistently low memory use suggests General Purpose may be enough.

rows.text: Reserved capacity discounts apply only to burst capacity above the baseline.
rows.why: Reserve the baseline; use on-demand pricing for bursts.

questions.hint: Low steady usage means you may be paying for more than you need.

questions.q: Single vector queries are slow, and memory pressure is causing heavy disk I/O. The server isn't yet at its tier's maximum size, and total query volume is modest. What does Learn suggest first?

options.text: Add a cache in front of the database
options.why: Caching helps with repeated reads at high volume, not with slow single queries caused by memory pressure.

options.text: Scale up to a larger server
options.why: Correct. Scale up when single-query latency is high, memory pressure causes disk I/O, and you haven't hit the tier's limits.

options.text: Add read replicas
options.why: Replicas help when total volume is high. These queries are slow one at a time.

options.text: Partition the table by tenant
options.why: Partitioning helps very large tables with a natural partition key, which isn't the problem here.

questions.hint: Is the problem total volume, or each query on its own?
questions.explain: Scale up when single-query latency is too high, memory pressure causes disk I/O, or you're below the tier maximum. Scale out (replicas or caching) when total volume exceeds one server or the workload is read-heavy with acceptable staleness.

questions.q: With PgBouncer in transaction mode, a query needs hnsw.ef_search = 200 for one high-accuracy search. How should the code set it?

options.text: SET LOCAL hnsw.ef_search = 200 in the transaction
options.why: Correct. SET LOCAL applies to the current transaction and reverts afterwards, which is safe with pooling.

options.text: SET hnsw.ef_search = 200 once when the app first starts
options.why: Session settings don't persist across transactions in transaction mode.

options.text: Pass ef_search in the connection string to port 5432
options.why: Bypassing PgBouncer defeats the pooling.

options.text: ALTER SYSTEM SET hnsw.ef_search = 200
options.why: A server-wide change affects every query.

questions.hint: In transaction mode, a plain SET might not stay on your connection. Scope the setting to the transaction.
questions.explain: Use SET LOCAL for per-query work_mem, ef_search or probes with pooled connections.

questions.q: Ten app instances share a database that allows 1,000 connections. Following Learn's guidance, what maximum pool size should each instance use?

options.text: About 100, leaving headroom
options.why: Correct. Cap each instance at the database limit divided by the number of instances, with headroom.

options.text: 10 each
options.why: That's far smaller than needed and causes waiting.

options.text: 1,000 each
options.why: Ten instances at 1,000 each would far exceed the limit.

options.text: 5,000 each through PgBouncer
options.why: max_client_conn is a PgBouncer client setting, not each app pool's maximum.

questions.hint: Divide the server's connection limit across instances, and leave some headroom.
questions.explain: Max pool size per instance ≈ database connections ÷ instances.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. An app moves from direct connections to PgBouncer in transaction mode.

rows.text: A LISTEN/NOTIFY channel for cache invalidation keeps working.
rows.why: LISTEN/NOTIFY requires persistent connections and doesn't work with transaction pooling.

rows.text: A named prepared statement from one transaction might not exist in the next.
rows.why: Different server connections may be assigned between transactions.

rows.text: Settings applied with plain SET persist for the rest of the client session.
rows.why: Session variables reset between transactions; use SET LOCAL.

rows.text: Retries for OperationalError should add random jitter to the backoff.
rows.why: Jitter stops instances retrying at the same moment.

questions.hint: Transaction mode hands connections around, so session-level features break.
questions.explain: Transaction pooling cuts connections but changes session behavior.
